title: Machine learning detection of small Strombolian eruptions in noisy multitemporal infrared images: Toward continuous monitoring
content:
Abstract
We show that a convolutional neural network (CNN) trained on denoised multitemporal infrared images (single images whose red, green, and blue channels hold three consecutive frames so that change between them appears as color) can detect small Strombolian eruptions that previously fell below the detection limits of conventional automated methods. Strombolian eruptions at Mount Erebus, Antarctica, range from large eruptions that eject lava throughout the crater to small eruptions that are mostly contained within the lake. We built these images from thermal imagery of the Ray lava lake and trained a CNN to classify them into three categories: “no eruption,” “small eruption,” and “large eruption.” A training and verification dataset of more than 54,000 images was built through a three-stage process, Clean  →  Expanded  →  Denoised, starting from a curated set of eruptions. We applied confident learning (Cleanlab) with five iterations of 5-fold Stratified Group K-Fold cross-validation. On the held-out test set, the denoised model achieved a macro F1 of 0.9782, Matthews correlation coefficient = 0.9397, and macro area under the receiver operating characteristic curve = 0.9981. To test temporal generalization, we applied the model to all December 2015 images, recorded over 10 months after the latest training images, during which the lake’s morphology changed. The network detected 49 large and 420 small eruptions. Manual verification of all detections and 2,461 stratified-sampled “no eruption” frames confirmed per-class precision of 0.98 for “large eruption” and 0.97 for “small eruption,” with a population-weighted macro F1 of 0.93.
